chapters.relation: This file bundles three essays. Kevin de Laplante reads Paul Chadwick's Concrete story 'Stay Tuned for Pearl Harbor', treating Concrete's angry monologue about oil companies and overpopulation as enlightened anthropocentrism, while Maureen's silent reverie of merging her body with root systems and being 'raped' by bulldozers dramatizes Arne Naess's deep-ecological expanded self and an ecofeminist link between the oppression of nature-as-female and of women; the utilitarianism of Bentham and Mill and Leopold's 'think like a mountain' land ethic frame the anthropocentrism/nonanthropocentrism debate. Pierre Skilling reads The Adventures of Tintin through Montesquieu's and Aristotle's typologies of government, casting Marshal Kurvi-Tasch's Borduria as Arendt-style totalitarianism (a secret police as true executive, a bid for world domination) against the legitimate monarchy of King Muskar XII, whose Syldavian sceptre works as a check on royal power. Terry Kading argues that 9/11 collapsed the superhero genre's binary of good versus evil into reality: bin Laden's 'monomaniacs' act as supervillains with a murky agenda, yet Spider-Man, Captain America and Superman comics concede no real superhero can rescue us, leaving only ordinary heroism and the compromised politics of national security.

holes.name: Montesquieu
holes.what: Enlightenment political theorist (1689-1755) known for the typology of republican, monarchical and despotic government and the separation of powers.
holes.why: Skilling's essay on The Good Government According to Tintin is built almost entirely on Montesquieu's classification of regimes and his 'power should be a check to power' doctrine, and the taxonomy has no matching philosopher slug.

holes.name: Separation of Powers and Forms of Government
holes.what: Montesquieu's distinction between moderate governments (monarchy, republic) and despotism, and the division of state power into legislative, executive and judiciary branches that check one another.
holes.why: The Tintin essay applies this framework directly to Syldavia, Borduria and San Theodoros, and the taxonomy offers no concept for Montesquieu's regime typology or separation of powers.
